$comment: Worked storyboards, as reference material for the agent — NOT one-click films.
Every `scene` is a real, valid Excalidraw scene made entirely of PLACEHOLDERS: dashed
cards carrying customData.placeholder, a caption under each, a frame per shot, and a
populated timeline. Nothing in them was generated and nothing in them costs anything
to open. validate_scene.py --templates runs over all of them in CI, so the examples
the agent copies from cannot quietly drift out of the contract.
A placeholder is not a clip and never becomes one on its own. Adopting a template
means: read each placeholder's prompt, adapt it to what the person actually asked
for, generate the shot, place the job in that position, and remove the placeholder.
The validator refuses a placeholder in a real scene for exactly this reason.
`prompt` is the sentence the person would say, and it is the only part usable as-is.
`assumes` says what the storyboard was written for. `adapt` says what usually differs
and what to do about it — both travel with the template into the first turn, so they
are written as instructions to the agent rather than notes to a reader.
`sample` is frame id -> TONE, for the preview card and nothing else. Not frames: a
poster that looked like real footage would sell the template on a shot nobody has
been asked to make yet, and the person would judge the result against a picture
nobody promised. A preview can honestly show the shape — how many shots, how long
each runs, the aspect, the palette. It cannot honestly show the film.
There is no 'blank' template, because a blank template is the absence of one: the
landing's prompt box already starts a video with no plan attached.
Every shot is 6 seconds because 6 s is the cheapest length every working video model
renders, and one of them renders only 6 s and 10 s. This is not a style choice and it
is not permanent: ask what the capabilities are and use what is available today.

templates.name: Product launch
templates.description: Six shots that reveal one object, show what it is made of, and end on the mark.
templates.prompt: Make me a 36-second launch film for our product — a reveal, the detail, it in someone's hands, it working, and the logo at the end.
templates.assumes: ONE object that photographs well, described in enough detail to draw — material, size, colour, what it does. A person appears in shots 3 and 5, as a hand and then a face, and it is the SAME person, which is what makes them a continuity problem. Shot 6 leaves the centre clear for a mark rather than generating one. Six shots of six seconds, 36 s, 16:9.
templates.adapt: The SHAPE that survives is the order: reveal, detail, human scale, proof, reaction, mark. Almost everything else changes. If the product is software there is nothing to photograph — replace shots 1 and 2 with the interface in use and say so, rather than generating a plausible object that is not theirs. If they have no person to feature, cut shots 3 and 5 and make it a four-shot film; four honest shots beat six with a stranger in them. If they do, generate that person ONCE as a still, show it, and make both shots from it — the same words run twice return two different faces and the film looks fine shot by shot and wrong end to end. Shot 6 is where people ask for a logo: generate the field and the light and tell them to drop the mark on afterwards, because a model asked for a specific logo produces something close enough to be embarrassing. Six seconds is a floor rather than a choice — check what the video capability can actually render today, because one model offers only 6 s and 10 s.

templates.name: Explainer
templates.description: Four shots and a narration line each: the problem, the idea, the fix, the same desk clear.
templates.prompt: Explain what we do in about 25 seconds — start with the problem, show the idea, show it working, and end where we started but fixed. With a voiceover.
templates.assumes: A problem with a VISIBLE form — shots 1 and 4 are the same frame before and after, and an invisible problem (latency, risk, compliance) gives them nothing to photograph. Four narration lines, one per shot, about twelve words each, written by the person or agreed with them first. Four shots of six seconds, 24 s, 16:9.
templates.adapt: Shots 1 and 4 are the same frame twice and that repetition is the argument — keep the angle, the light and the lens identical or the ending stops landing. If the problem has no visible form, do not reach for a stock metaphor; ask what their customer actually sees on a bad day and film that. Narration is the risk in this template: the speech models answer a prompt rather than reading it, so wrap every line in an instruction to read it exactly, generate ONE line first, and read back the transcript the job returns before generating the rest. If it will not read verbatim, say so and offer the film with captions instead — an improvised voiceover under someone's explainer is worse than silence. Twelve words is about six seconds of speech; longer lines run past their shot.

templates.name: Social teaser
templates.description: Three vertical shots that open on the ending and work backwards.
templates.prompt: Give me an 18-second vertical teaser — open on the payoff with no context, cut back to show how it started, then the turn.
templates.assumes: An end state legible in ONE second with no setup — if it needs explaining, this structure does not work and a straight three-beat does. Vertical throughout, with the lower third of the last shot left clear for a caption added elsewhere. Three shots of six seconds, 18 s, 9:16.
templates.adapt: Vertical is the whole constraint. Say 'vertical', 'portrait framing', 'subject in the middle third' in EVERY prompt: a model given no instruction returns a wide frame, and the export letterboxes it into black bars down both sides. Set 9:16 on the timeline as well, and check the first clip's real dimensions when it lands before generating the other two. If the payoff needs a sentence to make sense, drop this structure and tell the person why rather than shipping a hook nobody reads.

templates.name: Story
templates.description: Five shots with one character: a place, an arrival, a noticing, the thing, a decision.
templates.prompt: Tell a 30-second story with one character — they arrive somewhere, notice something, and decide what to do about it.
templates.assumes: ONE character, in shots 2, 3 and 5. This is the template that fails silently: three shots of the same person is three chances to get a different person, and a character image must exist BEFORE any of them is generated. One location, one time of day. Five shots of six seconds, 30 s, 16:9.
templates.adapt: The story shape holds for almost any subject — a customer, a founder, a delivery, an animal. What does not survive carelessness is the face. Generate the character once, show it, get a yes, and make shots 2, 3 and 5 FROM that image; a text prompt run three times returns three people and the film is unusable in a way that looks fine shot by shot. If the person said 'this character' and no image of them exists, stop and ask rather than inventing a lead you are then stuck with. Shots 1 and 4 have nobody in them and can go straight to a clip from text. If they want two characters, say that this structure holds one and offer a six-shot version — two half-established characters in thirty seconds is neither.

templates.name: How-to
templates.description: Five shots that show a method: the promise, the parts, the step, the change, the result.
templates.prompt: Show how our thing is made in about 30 seconds — the finished result first, then what goes into it and the step that matters, overhead, hands only.
templates.assumes: A procedure with two or three VISIBLE steps, filmed overhead on one surface in one light. Hands appear in shots 3 and 4 and are the recurring subject, so they are a continuity problem exactly like a face. Shots 1 and 5 are bookends of the same finished thing. Five shots of six seconds, 30 s, 16:9.
templates.adapt: The order is the argument: promise, parts, step, change, result. If the method has one step rather than two, cut shot 4 rather than inventing a second step — a fabricated step in a how-to is the one lie a viewer will actually try to follow. Hands recur, so generate them once as a still and make shots 3 and 4 from it; otherwise the sleeves, the skin and the surface change halfway through and it reads as two different people making two different things. Keep the camera overhead and the light identical across shots 2, 3 and 4 — the whole point is that only the material changes. Shots 1 and 5 must be the same finished thing: generate shot 1 first and make shot 5 from it.
